questions.q: What makes a known, scheduled spike (a product launch, a seasonal sale) the most plannable failure mode in capacity engineering, per this lesson?
options: It never actually requires any additional capacity beyond routine forecasting
It only affects marketing systems, never core production infrastructure
Because it isn't a surprise — the date and often the expected magnitude are known in advance, unlike routine organic growth
It is impossible to estimate in advance, so no planning is useful
questions.explain: Unlike routine growth trends, a scheduled event has a known date and an estimable magnitude from signals like a prior year's equivalent event, which makes it uniquely plannable — teams that still get caught by it usually never turned that plannability into an actual written, dated plan.

questions.q: What should a real pre-scaling plan's steps have, according to this lesson?
options: No fixed timeline, since capacity can always be added instantly
A specific owner and a date, worked backward from the event date, accounting for provisioning lead time
Approval from every engineer in the company before any step can proceed
A requirement that all steps happen simultaneously on the day of the event
questions.explain: A real pre-scaling plan works backward from the event date with each step dated and owned, so provisioning actions with real lead time (quota increases, replica scaling) actually clear before the event rather than during it.

questions.q: Why should the load test for a known spike be built around the event's exact expected request mix rather than a generic load test?
options: A generic load test is always more accurate than an event-specific one
Generic load tests are prohibited by most testing frameworks
Event-specific load tests are only relevant for mobile applications
A flash of traffic hitting a launch page behaves nothing like the steady-state traffic a generic load test usually models, so a generic test can miss exactly the behavior that matters for this event
questions.explain: A launch-day or flash-sale traffic pattern is structurally different from steady-state traffic. Applying the realistic-traffic discipline specifically to this event's expected mix and magnitude is what actually predicts how the system will behave during it.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should already exist before a known spike begins, not during it?
options: Event-specific dashboards, tuned alert thresholds, a staffed war room or escalation path, and feature flags/kill switches to shed non-essential load
A decision about whether the event will be postponed
A public apology prepared in case of an outage
A requirement that the on-call engineer build dashboards live during the event
questions.explain: The goal is for the first sign of trouble to come from a dashboard, not a customer — which requires event-specific dashboards, tuned alerting, a staffed escalation path, and ready kill switches to all exist before the spike starts, not be improvised during it.

questions.q: Why does a complete spike plan include a de-scale step and a rollback path, not just a scale-up step?
options: Because scaling up is always risk-free and never needs a rollback

Because pre-provisioned capacity left running indefinitely after the event raises cost, and a predefined rollback lets a team reverse a specific pre-scaling action calmly instead of improvising a fix live during the event
Because de-scaling and rollback steps are purely optional and rarely included in real plans
Because rollback plans are only relevant to disaster recovery, never to capacity planning
questions.explain: A complete plan scales capacity back down once the event ends to control ongoing cost, and defines in advance how to reverse any single pre-scaling action that causes its own problem — the same calm-in-advance discipline as a DR runbook, rather than inventing a fix under pressure.
